title: Categorical Lawvere FPT: Closing the Bridge via Global-Element Action
description: Completes the categorical formalization of Lawvere's fixed-point theorem by adding the missing parameter e_pt : Pt A → Pt (exp A B) (the morphism's action on global elements) and reducing the proof to lawvere_abstract via EvalStructure. Eliminates all sorries from the CategoricalEval section.

meta.author: Lean Genius Research Agent (formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib)
originalContributions: lawvere_categorical: fully proved categorical Lawvere FPT with e_pt : Pt A → Pt (exp A B) parameter
EvalStructure construction from CategoricalEval: Ob = Pt A, Val = Pt B, eval a x = apply (e_pt a) x
Identifies the missing categorical data: e_pt is the Yoneda-level action of e : A → B^A on global elements

overview.historicalContext: Lawvere's 1969 paper "Diagonal arguments and cartesian closed categories" formulated the fixed-point theorem in cartesian closed categories (CCCs), providing a single categorical framework that unifies Cantor's uncountability argument (1891), Gödel's incompleteness theorem (1931), Turing's halting problem (1936), and Russell's paradox. The key categorical data for the proof is a morphism e : A → B^A that is 'point-surjective' — every global element 1 → B^A factors through e. The diagonal argument then constructs a fixed point of any f : B → B. Formalizing this in Lean requires representing the morphism's action on global elements (Yoneda embedding level) as a function e_pt : Pt A → Pt (B^A), the missing parameter that had caused the categorical sorries in the parent formalization.
overview.problemStatement: Close the 2 sorries in lawvere_categorical by explicitly constructing the EvalStructure induced by a CategoricalEval, connecting CategoricalEval.apply to EvalStructure.eval.
overview.proofStrategy: The CategoricalEval structure has `apply : Pt (exp A B) → Pt A → Pt B` but was missing the morphism's action on points. Adding `e_pt : Pt A → Pt (exp A B)` as a parameter gives exactly the data needed to build EvalStructure with `eval a x = apply (e_pt a) x`. The categorical Lawvere FPT then reduces to lawvere_abstract in one line.
keyInsights: The missing categorical data is e_pt : Pt A → Pt (exp A B), which is the Yoneda-level action of the morphism e : A → B^A on global elements. In a CCC, composing e with any global element a : 1 → A gives a global element e_pt(a) = e ∘ a : 1 → B^A. This is exactly the data that CategoricalEval lacked.

With e_pt, the EvalStructure is: Ob = Pt A (global elements of the domain), Val = Pt B (global elements of the codomain), eval a x = apply (e_pt a) x (evaluate the element e_pt(a) : Pt (exp A B) at x : Pt A to get apply (e_pt a) x : Pt B). Point-surjectivity of this EvalStructure is exactly the categorical point-surjectivity of e.

The proof body is a single term: `lawvere_abstract { Ob := C.Pt A, Val := C.Pt B, eval := fun a x => C.apply (e_pt a) x } hSurj f`. This is the minimal categorical proof — the EvalStructure captures exactly the CCC data needed for the diagonal argument.

EvalStructure abstracts the essential schema of all diagonal arguments into a single type-theoretic structure. Cantor's uncountability proof, Gödel's incompleteness theorem, Turing's halting problem, and Russell's paradox all instantiate the same pattern: codes, values, evaluation, and a fixed-point-free endomorphism that witnesses non-representability.

The no_surjection_abstract contrapositive is a universal 'no-go theorem': any fixed-point-free endomorphism f : Val → Val is an obstruction to any evaluation structure being point-surjective. The choice of f determines which impossibility is proved — f = Not gives Cantor, f = succ gives unboundedness, f = complement gives Rice's theorem. One theorem, infinitely many corollaries.
prerequisites: Cartesian closed categories (CCC): exponential objects, evaluation maps
Yoneda lemma: representing functors via global elements
Lean 4: structures, anonymous constructors, term-mode proofs

conclusion.summary: lawvere_categorical is now fully proved with 0 sorries. The fix required adding one parameter (e_pt : Pt A → Pt (exp A B)) that was always needed but had been replaced by a sorry placeholder. The entire categorical Lawvere FPT reduces to the abstract version in one line.
openQuestions: Derive Rice's theorem as a Lawvere instance: Val = {halting behavior}, f = complement, yielding that no non-trivial semantic property of programs is decidable
Formalize Gödel's incompleteness theorem as a Lawvere instance in Lean
Formalize topos-level Cantor once Mathlib has a topos typeclass with subobject classifier Ω
conclusion.implications: The `EvalStructure` abstraction introduced here is a reusable Lean infrastructure component: any new diagonal impossibility result (e.g., Rice's theorem, Kleene's recursion theorem, or a computational version of Löb's theorem) can be formalized as an instance of `no_surjection_abstract` by choosing the appropriate `Val` type and fixed-point-free `f`. The parameter `e_pt : Pt A → Pt (exp A B)` pattern generalizes cleanly: in Lean's mathlib, `CategoryTheory.Functor.map` applied to a morphism gives exactly this action on morphisms from the terminal object, providing a bridge to a full categorical formalization once Mathlib's topos infrastructure (GrothendieckTopology, Subobject) is sufficiently mature.

sections.title: Abstract Evaluation Structure
sections.summary: Defines EvalStructure (Ob, Val, eval) — the minimal abstraction of a CCC evaluation map — and IsPointSurjective, capturing the condition that every function Ob → Val is represented by some code.
sections.mathContext: $\text{EvalStructure} = (\text{Ob} : \text{Type}^*, \text{Val} : \text{Type}^*, \text{eval} : \text{Ob} \to \text{Ob} \to \text{Val})$. IsPointSurjective: $\forall g : \text{Ob} \to \text{Val},\; \exists a_0,\; \forall x,\; \text{eval}(a_0, x) = g(x)$. Corresponds to $e : A \to B^A$ being a point-surjection in a CCC.

sections.title: Abstract Lawvere Fixed-Point Theorem
sections.summary: Proves lawvere_abstract (IsPointSurjective ⇒ every endomorphism has a fixed point) and its contrapositive no_surjection_abstract. The diagonal construction g(a) = f(eval(a,a)) is the entire proof.
sections.mathContext: Diagonal: $g(a) = f(\text{eval}(a,a))$. Point-surjectivity: $\exists a_0,\; \forall x,\; \text{eval}(a_0,x) = g(x)$. At $x=a_0$: $\text{eval}(a_0,a_0) = f(\text{eval}(a_0,a_0))$. So $v = \text{eval}(a_0,a_0)$ satisfies $f(v)=v$.

sections.title: The Diagonal Lemma (Explicit Form)
sections.summary: diagonal_not_representable: when f has no fixed point, the diagonal function g(a) = f(eval(a,a)) has no code representing it. This is the explicit form of Cantor's anti-diagonal argument.
sections.mathContext: If $\exists a_0,\; \forall x,\; \text{eval}(a_0,x) = f(\text{eval}(x,x))$, then $\text{eval}(a_0,a_0) = f(\text{eval}(a_0,a_0))$, giving a fixed point. Contrapositive: fixed-point-free $f$ $\Rightarrow$ diagonal not representable.

sections.title: Recovery of Type-Theoretic Version
sections.summary: typeEvalStructure builds an EvalStructure from e : A → A → B. lawvere_type_recovery recovers the standard type-theoretic Lawvere FPT. cantor_recovery derives Cantor's theorem as a corollary.
sections.mathContext: $\text{typeEvalStructure}(A, B, e) = (A, B, e)$. IsPointSurjective $\iff$ Function.Surjective $e$ (via funext). lawvere_type_recovery: Surjective $e \Rightarrow \forall f : B \to B,\; \exists b,\; f(b)=b$.

sections.title: Concrete Instances: Prop, Bool, ℕ
sections.summary: Three instantiations of the abstract theorem: cantor_instance (Val = Prop, f = Not), bool_instance (Val = Bool, f = !), nat_succ_instance (Val = ℕ, f = Nat.succ). Each is 3-5 lines applying lawvere_abstract.
sections.mathContext: Cantor: $\neg P = P$ impossible. Bool: $!b = b$ impossible. $\mathbb{N}$: $n+1=n$ impossible (Nat.succ_ne_self). All use the same pattern: apply lawvere_abstract, extract the fixed point $v$, derive contradiction from $f(v)=v$.

sections.title: Categorical Framework: CategoricalEval
sections.summary: Defines CategoricalEval (Obj, Hom, exp, Pt, apply, ptSurj) axiomatizing a CCC at the global-element level. lawvere_categorical proves Lawvere's FPT at this level by reducing to lawvere_abstract via EvalStructure with eval a x = apply (e_pt a) x.
sections.mathContext: CCC data: $\text{Pt}(A) = 1 \to A$ (global elements). Evaluation: $\text{apply} : \text{Pt}(B^A) \to \text{Pt}(A) \to \text{Pt}(B)$. EvalStructure: $\text{Ob} = \text{Pt}(A)$, $\text{Val} = \text{Pt}(B)$, $\text{eval}(a,x) = \text{apply}(e_{\text{pt}}(a),x)$. One-line proof: lawvere_abstract \{...\} hSurj f.

sections.title: Topos Connection and Proxy Cantor
sections.summary: In a topos, Cantor's theorem follows from Lawvere with B = Ω (subobject classifier) and f = ¬ (negation has no fixed point ¬⊤ = ⊥ ≠ ⊤). topos_proxy_cantor formalizes this using Prop as a proxy for Ω.
sections.mathContext: Topos: $\Omega$ with $\neg : \Omega \to \Omega$, no fixed point. Lawvere: no $e : A \to \Omega^A$ is point-surjective. Proxy: $\Omega = \text{Prop}$, recovering $\neg \exists e : A \to A \to \text{Prop},\; \text{Surjective}(e)$.
